finding.claim: Shared-access grants can never be revoked: the owner can add users to a note's shared list but no endpoint removes them, so access persists for the life of the note.
finding.source: Owner's POST body field request.json["user"] on /n/<nid>/share
finding.sink: n["shared"].append(...) at notes.py:45, which grants read access via can_view at notes.py:8

trace.note: append user to shared list; no removal path exists in the file
can_view keeps granting access to any entry in shared

finding.guards_checked: Owner-only check via require_edit/can_edit (notes.py:17, 44). No unshare or revoke endpoint exists in the file, so there is no lifetime bound on a grant.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit at notes.py:20-22,44 restricts /share to the owner. can_view at notes.py:8 is the read gate the grant feeds into.
verdict.reason: The trace lines (notes.py:41, 43, 44, 45, 8) are accurate and no revoke route exists in notes.py or any other file in the directory, but the only actor who can reach the append is the note owner (notes.py:44), who already has full authority to grant read access, so no privilege is gained; the lack of revocation is a missing feature rather than an authorization bypass.

finding.claim: The share endpoint stores unvalidated principals, including null, into the ACL. If g.user is None for anonymous requests, can_view(None, note) grants read access to notes that contain a null entry.
finding.source: request.json["user"] on /n/<nid>/share, with no type or null check
finding.sink: ACL membership test user in note["shared"] at notes.py:8

trace.note: null or non-string principal appended to shared
read path passes g.user into require_view
can_view returns true when user is None and shared contains None

finding.guards_checked: Only the owner can reach the append (require_edit at notes.py:44), so direct impact is limited to the owner's own note. Whether g.user can be None for anonymous requests is not visible in this file and must be confirmed in the auth layer.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22, called at notes.py:44) is an effective owner-only guard: it aborts with 403 on failure, so only the note owner reaches the append at line 45. No type or null validation of request.json["user"] exists at line 45. No auth or before_request layer exists in the directory, so how g.user is set for anonymous requests is not visible.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: line 45 appends an unchecked value, line 28 passes g.user to require_view, and notes.py:8 returns true for user None when shared contains None. But the attacker must be the note's owner (require_edit at notes.py:44), and the exploit requires g.user to be None for anonymous requests, which is set in an auth layer not present in this directory, so the outcome cannot be decided from the available code.

finding.claim: Note existence can be enumerated: a missing note ID returns a 500 from an unhandled KeyError, while an existing note the caller cannot view returns 403, so the two responses differ.
finding.source: URL path segment nid on /n/<nid> (also on PUT and share routes)
finding.sink: NOTES[nid] dictionary lookup at notes.py:27, 34, 43 (KeyError for missing IDs) versus abort(403) at notes.py:13, 36, 22

trace.note: NOTES[nid] raises KeyError for an unknown ID, giving HTTP 500
require_view aborts with 403 for an existing note the caller cannot view

finding.guards_checked: Authorization checks themselves are correct; the flaw is the differing response codes. Severity depends on how unpredictable note IDs are, which is not visible in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are require_view/can_view (notes.py:11-13) and can_edit/require_edit (notes.py:16-22). They run only after NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27, 34 and 43 has already raised KeyError for a missing ID. No errorhandler is registered in notes.py, so Flask returns 500. The 403 path (notes.py:13, 36, 22) is reached only for an existing note, so the two responses differ.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27 raises KeyError (500) for a missing ID before require_view at notes.py:28 can abort with 403 at notes.py:13 for an existing note the caller cannot view, so any caller who reaches these routes can tell the two cases apart. This is a low-severity existence oracle, and its real impact depends on how unguessable note IDs are, which this file does not show. The 403 path also assumes g.user is set by middleware outside this file.

finding.claim: Any user with view access receives the full note object, including the shared list, which exposes the identities of every other sharee.
finding.source: Any authenticated user who passes require_view on /n/<nid>
finding.sink: jsonify(n) at notes.py:29 returns the entire note, including the shared field

trace.note: jsonify returns n including the shared list

finding.guards_checked: View check is correct (require_view at notes.py:11-13 via can_view). Only the disclosure of the shared list is at issue; this may be intended behavior.

verdict.guard_found: require_view at notes.py:11-13 (via can_view at notes.py:7-8) is an effective abort(403) gate for the view check, but it only controls who may read the note. Nothing between notes.py:28 and notes.py:29 filters the response, so jsonify(n) returns the full note dict, including the "shared" list (and "owner"). No field-level redaction exists in the file.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: require_view at notes.py:28 passes for a sharee, and jsonify(n) at notes.py:29 returns the whole note, including the shared list. A sharee reaches this legitimately, so the finding is a low-severity information disclosure of co-sharee identities rather than an authorization bypass, and it stands unless the design intends the sharee list to be private (not determinable from this file).

finding.claim: The shared list has no dedupe, size cap, or type validation on the user value, so the owner can grow it without bound and store non-string JSON values. Every can_view call scans the list linearly.
finding.source: request.json["user"] on /n/<nid>/share, repeatable by the owner
finding.sink: n["shared"].append(...) at notes.py:45, with the linear scan at notes.py:8

trace.note: append accepts any JSON value with no dedupe or cap
membership test is O(len(shared)) on every read and write

finding.guards_checked: Only the owner can append (require_edit at notes.py:44). Impact is resource growth and data quality, not an authorization bypass.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22) restricts the append at notes.py:45 to the note owner. No dedupe, cap, or type check exists on the appended value, so the code-level claims are accurate.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (append at notes.py:45, linear membership test at notes.py:8, owner-only gate at notes.py:44 via require_edit), but the only actor who can reach the append is the note owner, who already has full control of that note's sharing list, so unbounded growth only degrades the owner's own note and grants no new power. This is a quality or self-DoS issue, not a security vulnerability.
